stories.topic: The CXO who has nothing to talk about
stories.summary: A friend of Amit's, a CXO at a big company, complains that evenings with fellow C-suite executives are deadly dull. None of them read books, watch world cinema, or care about world affairs or history, so conversation loops through cricket, Bollywood and office gossip. Amit reckons about ninety-five percent of people live in a groove like this.
stories.insight: Seniority and success don't make people interesting; self-reflection and curiosity do. Without them, people stop growing. As Amit puts it via Dylan, they are busy dying.
stories.quote: They don't read books, they don't watch world cinema, they're not interested in world affairs or history or any of that stuff.

stories.topic: Six classes in three years: the self-taught polymath
stories.summary: Amit's degree is a BA in English Literature from Fergusson College, Pune. He picked it because he knew he wouldn't have to study, and says he attended about six classes across three years. His real education was obsessive reading. Steven Pinker's The Blank Slate opened up natural selection for him, and he went on to read all of Dawkins, Daniel Dennett and Robert Wright. Hazlitt, Bastiat and popular economics books did the same for economics. Five years of professional poker taught him probabilistic thinking.
stories.insight: Formal credentials aren't the gate. Once a field's first principles click (scarcity, incentives, natural selection), the rest of the field opens up, and you can carry the tools elsewhere. Amit has used economic thinking to break down cricket strategy.
stories.quote: I only chose English literature because I knew I wouldn't have to study.

stories.topic: Walking away from being a company man
stories.summary: Around 2006–07 Amit was managing editor of Cricinfo. He decided he would never hold a job again, moved to a contributing-editor consulting role for a couple of years, then left entirely. Since then he has written a book, played professional poker for five years, and edited the policy magazine Pragati for the Takshashila Institution, remotely and part-time.
stories.insight: The choice didn't always look like good fortune. It bought him the key input for a learning life: control over his time, so he can read what he wants, when he wants, without being pushed down a corporate track.
stories.quote: I decided some seventeen years ago that I'm never gonna do a job again. I'm never gonna work in a company or be a company man.

stories.topic: A life lived through one global drama after another
stories.summary:
Ajay never accepted the narrow specialise-and-publish track. As a PhD student he read biology on the side for the pleasure of it. Looking back, his life has been a series of deep dives into world crises:
- the Asian crisis
- 9/11, Islamic extremism and the Afghanistan wars
- the 2008 financial crisis
- the pandemic
- the rise of modern populism

Reading about the Great Depression, he says, is different from living through a crisis yourself: watching the data, knowing who said what on which date, and being surprised when the VIX crossed 68.
stories.insight: Broad building blocks across science, statistics, economics and history work as entry gates. With them, each unfolding world event becomes a live seminar rather than a headline.
stories.quote: So I'm the child of all these big global dramatic events that happened.

stories.summary: While staying with his friend Mohit Satyanand in Delhi, Amit gave him his usual lecture: start a newsletter, be bloody-minded, have a bias for action. Mohit started, and in roughly three years he hasn't missed a single Sunday.
stories.insight: A fixed, non-negotiable cadence turns 'someday' into a habit. A friend's nudge at the right moment can launch years of consistent work.
stories.quote: He started and since then he hasn't missed a Sunday.

stories.topic: A boat that never sailed and a pact to write books
stories.summary: At a conference in Kochi two years ago, Amit, Lancelot Pinto and Vasant Dhar were put on a boat for a ride. A storm started and the boat never left. Standing on board and talking about the books they each wanted to write, the three promised that all of them would have written one by the next year's conference. Amit had earlier pushed Vasant to start a newsletter in a personal tone, and then to write a book in that voice. Two years on, Vasant has just sent his final manuscript to his publisher. Amit and Lancelot, whenever they meet, marvel at Vasant and hope to be inspired by him.
stories.insight: Pacts among friends create accountability, but they only pay off for whoever actually does the work. Amit casts himself as the cautionary half of the story: a prolific weekly producer who keeps postponing the deep projects he cares about most.
stories.quote: by the time this conference comes about next year, all three of us would have written a book

stories.topic: From books by strangers to a shelf of signed copies
stories.summary: When Ajay was a child, the great books in the house were written by strange, mysterious people far away. Recently, at lunch with Akshay Jaitly, who is finishing what Ajay calls an absolutely grand book, the two marvelled that they now live among friends and family who write books. Both plan a shelf of nothing but signed copies.
stories.insight: An intellectual life matures when the books on your shelf stop coming from a distant priesthood and start coming from people you know. Being part of such a community is a blessing in itself.
stories.quote: we are embedded in the world of people building books and one after another, these are the passion projects of our friends and family, and we get signed copies of all these books.

stories.topic: Touring Spain with ChatGPT Deep Research
stories.summary: Travelling through Spain, Amit had ChatGPT Deep Research write reports of around twenty thousand words before each museum: the Picasso Museum, the Prado, the Reina Sofia. Each covered the artists' lives and phases, the key works in each room, and the order in which to walk through the rooms. Before a train from Barcelona to Madrid with a huge bag, he asked where to stow it. The AI asked which train, then told him which coach to board and where the luggage racks were at the start and end of the coach, with a photograph.
stories.insight: The AI's output is only as deep as your prompts, and your prompts are only as deep as your curiosity and prior knowledge. Amit treats it as a complete Google replacement but still checks the cited sources himself.
stories.quote: And a lot of it is how deeply you prompt.

stories.summary: Amit has recently seen several real cases of an elderly woman whose husband dies and who suddenly becomes a new person: free, learning an instrument, travelling solo. These women may never have thought of their marriages as confining, because marriage was the structure they flowed into, it was normalised, and no alternative ever seemed to exist.
stories.insight: An institution's cost can be invisible to the people inside it. Amit ties this to Chinmay Tumbe's finding that marriage drives the largest internal migration in India: women are uprooted from their villages and their friends, and sometimes even lose their names.
stories.quote: There's an old lady, her husband had died and suddenly she's like a new person. It's like she's free, she's blooming, she's learning an instrument, or she's travelling solo

recommendations.creator: Matthew Walker
recommendations.context: Cited when a listener asked for an episode shot at dawn, to explain why that's impossible for him.
recommendations.reason: He calls it an excellent book. It shows that roughly thirty percent of people are night owls whose natural rhythm is simply different, which explains 'the tyranny of the larks.'

recommendations.creator: Philip Tetlock and Dan Gardner
recommendations.context: His deliberate 'book recommendation middle of the episode,' made while discussing academics and pundits who perform certainty.
recommendations.reason: Tetlock shows that TV experts are often wrong, while the people who get things right are constantly doing Bayesian thinking and updating their priors. Amit wants that idea to spread more widely in society.

recommendations.creator: Steven Pinker
recommendations.context: Named as his gateway into natural selection.
recommendations.reason: It gave him the first principles of human nature and evolution. After it, the whole field opened up and reshaped his view of the world.

recommendations.item: Richard Dawkins's books, including The Selfish Gene and The Blind Watchmaker
recommendations.creator: Richard Dawkins
recommendations.context: Part of the evolution rabbit hole he went down after Pinker, along with Daniel Dennett and Robert Wright.
recommendations.reason: He read 'the whole shebang.' Understanding natural selection deeply changed how he sees human nature.

recommendations.creator: Henry Hazlitt
recommendations.context: Mentioned as an early economics book. Lant Pritchett told Amit on The Seen and the Unseen that it was one of his own formative books.
recommendations.reason: A first-principles entry into economic thinking. You don't need regressions, just the fundamentals of scarcity and incentives.

recommendations.creator: Frédéric Bastiat
recommendations.context: Something he read early in his economics self-education.
recommendations.reason: Part of the foundational reading that made economic first principles part of his mental framework.

recommendations.creator: Tim Harford
recommendations.context: Singled out among 'Tim Harford's great books' as a particularly good one.
recommendations.reason: Popular economics that shows how economic reasoning explains everyday life. Once you absorb such fundamentals, everything else starts to make sense.

recommendations.creator: Steven Pinker
recommendations.context: Cited in his thought experiment about a child raised without hearing language.
recommendations.reason: He calls it a great book on how the structures of language are built into the brain. Even so, a child who never hears words won't speak.

recommendations.creator: Chinmay Tumbe
recommendations.context: The source of one of the great 'TILs' from his years doing The Seen and the Unseen.
recommendations.reason: It shows that marriage drives the largest internal migration in India, which reveals how much identity women lose when they marry.

recommendations.creator: Aella
recommendations.context: One of the newsletters he pays for, which he offers as proof he really values it.
recommendations.reason: Strong data work on young people and their sexual lives. Aella draws on her experience as a sex worker and is also a very good data scientist, which gives real insight into modern society.

recommendations.creator: Signull
recommendations.context: He discovered the anonymous writer through a striking tweet and now pays a hundred dollars a year.
recommendations.reason: The quality of the content, which he finds genuinely thought-provoking.

recommendations.creator: Mohit Satyanand
recommendations.context: One of the newsletters Amit encouraged a friend to start and now enjoys.
recommendations.reason: About three years without missing a Sunday. Amit is very proud of him.

recommendations.creator: Vasant Dhar
recommendations.context: Amit urged Vasant to start it in a personal tone rather than making it only about the subject.
recommendations.reason: Amit believed the personal tone would really work. That voice has since grown into a finished book.

recommendations.creator: Vasant Dhar
recommendations.context: Vasant's podcast. Amit used to produce it; Gaurav Chintamani produces it now.
recommendations.reason: Mentioned warmly as the show of a very dear friend whose work Amit backs.

recommendations.creator: Shane Parrish
recommendations.context: A listener asked about mental models and mentioned Parrish and Charlie Munger.
recommendations.reason: 'Shane Parrish's books are great.' A good source for building a toolkit of mental models.

recommendations.creator: Charlie Munger
recommendations.context: Raised in the same question about mental models.
recommendations.reason: Munger has always been a source of great wisdom on how to think.

recommendations.creator: Radiohead
recommendations.context: A listener asked about people playing Radiohead's Creep on loop. Amit admitted he did the same in the early 90s.
recommendations.reason: There's so much more to Radiohead than Creep. 'Just' is also awesome, and its video is a masterpiece.

recommendations.item: Amit's column on the benefits of reading books
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Promised in the show notes in answer to 'what's the ultimate benefit of reading books?'
recommendations.reason: Sets out his argument that books multiply the dots we join to picture the world, letting us live many lives.

recommendations.creator: OpenAI
recommendations.context: Answering a question about how he uses LLMs. He also notes that Perplexity links its sources.
recommendations.reason: 'Off the charts good.' It asks clarifying questions, cites sources, writes deep custom reports, and has replaced Google for him. Your curiosity has to drive it, and you still verify the sources.

recommendations.context: How he manages knowledge and recalls quotes in the middle of episodes.
recommendations.reason: He keeps copious, well-organised notes in it and can search them instantly, which makes up for a memory he says isn't great.

recommendations.item: Professional cycling as a sport to follow
recommendations.context: A listener asked how he overcame his cricket addiction. The hosts have an episode on cycling.
recommendations.reason: It gives all the drama and stories of sport for far less time than cricket. Even a T20 game eats hours, and the IPL eats two months of evenings.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Discussed at length. Two cohorts are done (52 and 38 people), the third is in September, and an offline meetup in Goa is planned for late October.
recommendations.reason: It teaches the lessons they wish someone had taught them at twenty, starting with frameworks for looking at the world. Past cohorts have formed a community with city meetups and book clubs.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: A listener asked how to build an audience on Substack. The last cohort ran the previous October, and the waiting list is long.
recommendations.reason: His writing course, built on the philosophy of writing something good rather than chasing an audience.

recommendations.item: Everything is Everything episode: Fixing the Knowledge Society
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Pointed to when a listener asked about misinformation within academic research.
recommendations.reason: Covers exactly how incentives in academia push research in the wrong directions.

recommendations.item: Everything is Everything episode on economic fallacies
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Referenced twice: on zero-sum thinking, and on why statist intuitions persist.
recommendations.reason: He calls it 'a great episode.' It explains common fallacies that are hardwired into us, which helps when judging economists' debates.

recommendations.item: Everything is Everything episode on atheism
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Mentioned while explaining how he keeps his sense of humour in the face of mortality.
recommendations.reason: 'Awesome episode, I'm very proud of it.'

recommendations.item: Everything is Everything Episode 49 (on podcasting) and the productivity episode
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Six listeners asked how he remembers so much.
recommendations.reason: These are the episodes where he demonstrates his Roam Research note-taking system on screen.

recommendations.item: Everything is Everything episode on whether character is contingent
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Raised when a listener asked whether individuals can have independent identities.
recommendations.reason: Explores how a slight change in brain chemistry can make you a different person, as with Phineas Gage.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes as the show's earlier AMA.
recommendations.reason: The companion to this episode, recorded at the halfway mark.

core_ideas.concept: Speculate, but with transparency
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay worried about straying beyond his expertise. Amit's view of the show is to bring frames from one field to bear on another without pretending to be certain. You can talk usefully about things you're still learning, as long as you're open that you're speculating and exploring.
core_ideas.quote: you could be on a journey of discovery and you're sharing the enthusiasm of that journey with someone.

core_ideas.concept: Self-reflection is what sets thoughtful people apart
core_ideas.explanation: Most people, especially men, never reflect on why they do what they do or want what they want. Those who do enter a virtuous cycle: they improve themselves and seek out other reflective people who reinforce the habit. Yet we contain multitudes. Amit is thoughtful about ideas but on autopilot about his finances and his health.
core_ideas.quote: when you start self reflecting, when you internalize that, I think it then becomes a virtuous cycle

core_ideas.concept: Politicians are the entrepreneurs of the state
core_ideas.explanation: From Vijay Kelkar, Ajay learned that officials are trained into conservatism while politicians take risks. Politicians walk thousands of kilometres meeting real people and know far more about farm distress or jobs than their slogans suggest. Amit pushes back that politics is downstream of culture, so populist demand shapes populist supply. Ajay's answer is that great leadership means doing more than following the polls.
core_ideas.quote: All the major milestones in Indian history have been politicians rolling the dice and doing something new.

core_ideas.concept: Judging expert debates you can't follow technically
core_ideas.explanation:
Amit's checklist for weighing economists you can't fully follow:
- Apply the frameworks you do understand. Anyone treating inequality and poverty as the same thing is thinking in zero-sum terms.
- Be suspicious of people who toe a whole tribal package of positions.
- Notice incoherence, such as backing free markets while opposing personal freedom.
- Focus on arguments, not personalities. Ideas last; people die.
- Remember you don't have to hold an opinion at all.
core_ideas.quote: it is not imperative for me to have an opinion on it. You know? I can just wait and learn.

core_ideas.concept: Read constrained speech as the party line
core_ideas.explanation: People have different degrees of freedom to speak, depending on their institution. A Federal Reserve official, a party member, or anyone at a regulated financial firm is under pressure to conform. Their public statements reflect a negotiated consensus, so don't judge them by the standards of sharp logic. The person is often much better than their writing suggests.
core_ideas.quote: So don't judge them when you see their constrained writings, because actually there is a full bubbling mind behind there, but they're just living out the institutional constraints.

core_ideas.concept: Pride vs self-respect depends on where you start
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay calls pride a negative emotion that slides into hubris once you start inhaling your own press releases. Amit calls that 'a thinking male answer.' Citing Shrayana Bhattacharya, he notes that men tend toward unwarranted self-confidence and women toward unwarranted self-doubt. Men should watch their pride; many women need more of it.
core_ideas.quote: wake up every morning and look in the mirror and say, I am awesome.

core_ideas.concept: Think in probabilities; life is managing luck
core_ideas.explanation: Poker taught Amit to think in a Bayesian way, which made him less certain, less judgmental of others, and less proud of his own successes. People who perform certainty are either simplifying or are charlatans. The best forecasters keep updating their priors.
core_ideas.quote: I know that ninety nine percent of everything is luck. And it's a management of luck that is a key skill in both poker and life.

core_ideas.concept: High-powered incentives broke academic research
core_ideas.explanation: Publication bias rewards sensational results. Behavioural findings fail to replicate at the magnitudes originally claimed. Careers revolve around raising money and schmoozing editors. From 1900 to 1925, with almost no funding, field after field was revolutionised; million-fold increases in spending since then have disappointed. Ajay calls this a sobering lesson for economists: people chase exactly what you reward.
core_ideas.quote: when you put up really high powered incentives, the people will goddamn pursue them.

core_ideas.concept: First principles plus rabbit holes
core_ideas.explanation: You don't need technical training in a field. What matters is that its fundamentals (scarcity, incentives, natural selection) become part of how you think. The way to get there is to dive into whatever fascinates you, without asking what productive thing will come of it.
core_ideas.quote: If it's a rabbit hole, just get into the rabbit hole and the more you read and at some point the fog clears and you see the bigger picture

core_ideas.concept: Memory comes from volume and connections
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's retention is low, but he reads so much that what sticks still adds up to a lot, and Roam catches the rest. Ajay adds the idea of adjacencies. We remember knowledge that connects richly to what we already know; topology is far easier after calculus and real analysis. And every use of a memory refreshes it, like a static RAM cell.
core_ideas.quote: So if you just read a lot, the memorable stuff will stick with you, whether you take a note or not.

core_ideas.concept: Knowledge is a social project; solitude is for reflection
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay increasingly finds his work comes from arguing with people and being corrected by them, much like the early-20th-century physicists at Göttingen who argued about matter and energy while hiking together. Amit agrees you need people both to grow and to be happy. You also need solitude, as long as it goes into healthy self-reflection rather than wallowing.
core_ideas.quote: I'm constantly in a process of talking to other people, arguing with other people, and other people are fixing me up.

core_ideas.concept: Do the work; don't chase validation
core_ideas.explanation: Asking 'how do I build an audience?' first is a trap. Beginners are bad and get no audience; if validation matters to them, they quit and never get good. A good product is the best marketing. The same goes for fearing irrelevance or controversy, since both depend on how the world responds to you. The hosts committed to 104 episodes before judging the show, and Amit keeps putting episodes out despite having 'a face for audio.'
core_ideas.quote: You get good at it only by doing something bloody mindedly again and again and again without thinking about validation.

core_ideas.concept: Reading is collecting dots
core_ideas.explanation: We understand the world by joining dots, and personal experience can only supply so many. Each book lets you live another life, so your picture of the world becomes higher-definition, and so does your picture of yourself.
core_ideas.quote: we form a picture of the world by joining dots. And therefore the more dots there are, the more high definition our picture will be.

core_ideas.concept: Stock and flow
core_ideas.explanation: Flow is blogs and columns. It is valuable as thinking aloud and as a writing gym; Amit wrote about eight thousand blog posts from 2003 to 2008, though he considers none worth preserving. Stock is books, and he admits he hasn't produced enough of it. Ajay writes his columns and LEAP blog posts with a researcher's push for novelty, so they become reusable. A book then weaves those small inventions into one large tapestry.
core_ideas.quote: So I feel books are the leap of integration. Small inventions happen along the way.

core_ideas.concept: Money is blood; time is the real scarcity
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay: you need money to live, but it isn't how you keep score in the video game or the thing to maximise. Amit: when you're young, money feels like the binding constraint, but over a whole life, time is what you will definitely run out of.
core_ideas.quote: money is like blood. You need money to live, but it's not the point of living.

core_ideas.concept: There is no self apart from your influences
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's thought experiment: a child who hears no language for its first years won't speak at all. A child who hears only its parents gets a limited vocabulary and personality. Add television, playmates and books, and the self widens. Phineas Gage shows how fragile the self is. Even if free will is doubtful, you still choose your company, your reading and your influences, and those shape you.
core_ideas.quote: you cannot separate the individual from the context of the society that you're in.

core_ideas.concept: Climate change is a coordination problem, not a technology problem
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay says the energy revolution in solar, wind, nuclear and storage has worked, so with adequate carbon taxes the world can keep growing while decarbonising. The hard part is getting countries to cooperate on a global public good when each has an incentive to renege. Amit adds that France shows nuclear works, and warns that NGOs have a fundraising incentive to exaggerate the danger.
core_ideas.quote: if all the world would cooperate and you did the requisite carbon taxation, it's not that difficult to cope with this

core_ideas.concept: Unknown unknowns are a source of hope
core_ideas.explanation: Amit won't call anything about India's future inevitable. The world of 2040 can't be pictured today, and rapid change could undo the things he dislikes now. Ajay names two high-probability problems: a dramatic fall in fertility that will bring rapid ageing, and global warming that is already baked in.
core_ideas.quote: I find that the fact that it is unknown unknowns is actually a cause of hope

core_ideas.concept: Conventional marriage is misaligned with modernity
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's answer to which non-economic part of Indian life clashes with modernity. Women move to the husband's village, sometimes change their names, lose their childhood friends, and live in service of the husband. He grants that tradition offers reassurance and admits modern dating is complicated too.
core_ideas.quote: for most of India, except for elites like us, for most of India, I think marriage is death for women.

core_ideas.concept: The religion of the state
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay is optimistic that the statism born of the 1914–1945 crisis era is fading as India globalises and grows comfortable with markets. Amit, who meets more young people, thinks most still treat the state as mai-baap, expected to solve every problem and ban whatever offends. Because zero-sum, top-down intuitions are hardwired, each generation has to fight this battle again.
core_ideas.quote: India's default religion has been the religion of the state.

core_ideas.concept: Communities of choice over communities of circumstance
core_ideas.explanation: Both hosts grew up making friends with whoever lived nearby; the internet let them form communities by choice. Amit wonders whether nation-states will matter less to identity, even though they keep their coercive power. India has been a nation-state for only about seventy-eight years, and maps keep changing. Ajay notes that borders have softened over fifty years and calls state interference in voluntary cross-border deals a dumb idea.
core_ideas.quote: And the internet freed both of us, and certainly for me it's a very big deal that I could form communities of choice. And geography was no longer destiny

core_ideas.concept: Mortality puts every other problem in perspective
core_ideas.explanation: Asked how he stays funny, Amit says death is the fundamental tragedy, and as atheists the hosts take it seriously. Next to it every other tragedy shrinks, so stressing over an article becomes laughable. Ajay's version: since the end is certain, live fully and delight in being here.
core_ideas.quote: the world is a tragedy to those who feel a comedy to those who think.

core_ideas.concept: Play the hand you're dealt; reject victimhood
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay: everyone gets a random hand of cards, whether pretty or ugly, rich or poor, with or without books at home. The only interesting question is what you do next, not complaining about structural injustice. Amit: the worst thing you can do is wrap yourself in a narrative of victimhood, because your circumstances of birth don't define you.
core_ideas.quote: I was dealt a hand of cards, how do I make the best of it?

core_ideas.concept: As an X, contribute by doing X well
core_ideas.explanation: A software engineer asked how to contribute to the world. Ajay's advice: practise the craft, write good code, join open-source projects, and fuel others' passion. Amit generalises it: if people pay you for your work, you are adding value to their lives, and that is a respectable contribution. You don't need to go and feed the hungry.
core_ideas.quote: whenever there's a question with the structure, as an X, how can I contribute to the world? I'm like do X well.

core_ideas.concept: Labour unions as market power
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay sees a union as market power: a group saying take it or leave it. An open labour market with free entry and exit produces a Pareto-superior outcome. Amit defends the right to form unions, but says the 'evil capitalist versus poor worker' story often hurts workers more than it helps them.
core_ideas.quote: When you do collective bargaining implicit in it is the threat that all of us together will not show up to work tomorrow and the work of the company will shut down.

core_ideas.concept: The 70/30 rule for creative careers
core_ideas.explanation:
Amit spent his early years as a copywriter, an MTV scriptwriter and a journalist, which felt like a waiting room for creative greatness. His advice:
- If seventy percent of your work is drudgery and thirty percent satisfies you, you're lucky.
- Be bloody-minded about protecting that thirty percent.
- Bring care to the drudgery too, because that's where you learn the craft.
- As you succeed, don't let the ratio drift to 100/0 and lose the spark.
core_ideas.quote: You're very lucky to have that thirty percent.

core_ideas.concept: With closed-minded family, pick your battles
core_ideas.explanation: Share your views without preaching and gift good books. But with elders who won't budge, step back: love them for everything else and keep the relationship intact. Keep the humility to accept that you might be wrong. Among the friends you choose, bigotry and sexism are firm red lines.
core_ideas.quote: Because paradigms change one funeral at a time. People don't change their minds they die.

core_ideas.concept: A country can't be better than its elite
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay admires the generation that led the Congress through the freedom movement. Even so, he thinks India is building critical mass in intellectual capacity for the first time in a century, helped by the internet, across science, business, the humanities and policy. That is why he is optimistic. His advice to young people: find your people and the pleasure of thinking and building.
core_ideas.quote: A country cannot be better than its elite. It can be much worse than its elite, but we're growing really high capability in India today

core_ideas.concept: Judge AI by its trajectory, not today's snapshot
core_ideas.explanation: Amit thinks it is very early days for AI. Tools like Deep Research are already superb tutors and research aids, but they amplify your curiosity rather than replacing your thinking. Always go back to the sources.
core_ideas.quote: is like judging computing by looking at a mainframe computer that filled a room in nineteen fifty four.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Ajay's apology after a hundred episodes outside his expertise: 'I apologise to you, gentle reader. If I have on occasion misrepresented my standard errors.'

Ajay gushes about growing mushrooms ('my stomach is bursting with anticipation'), then admits, 'This is all theoretical. I haven't done it yet.' Amit: 'You must be a fungi.' Later Ajay says Arvind Modi's excitement about tax policy after forty years matches his own about mushrooms, 'and I haven't even grown any mushrooms.' Amit: 'Which is why you're excited.'

The running taxation-is-theft dig at Ajay's upcoming tax book. Amit starts, 'it is not a book about taxation alone, it is a book about theft, because taxation is', and Ajay cuts him off. Later, on friends with wrong opinions: 'people will say taxation is not theft. Or even write books about it.'

Amit the night owl accuses Ajay, a morning lark, of complicity in 'the tyranny of the larks' against 'my people, the unfortunate night owls': 'Waking up in the morning is just like animal cruelty at this point.'

After Ajay calls himself a child of the Asian crisis, 9/11, 2008 and the pandemic, Amit says: 'There's an old Chinese curse, may you live in interesting times. For you it seems a blessing which can only mean you're a sociopath.'

Asked whether a show like this was inevitable in modern India, Amit rejects the Marxian view in favour of the great man theory. The tides of history, he says, wouldn't produce two other people like them, because 'There are no people like us.'
Amit on moving from an audio show to video: 'I have a face for audio.'
Amit admits he keeps repeating Dylan's 'he not busy being born is busy dying'. When that happens he curses himself for not reading enough, for not having 'enough new things coming into my LLM.'

Asked for hair-care advice, Amit plugs a daily 'quotidian' shampoo from Bath and Body Works, then adds: 'I should be the last fucking influencer you look at for hair.' Ajay claims the scene where Amit ruffled his hair 'made waves.' Amit: 'No, it has not made waves. I also know how to look at the analytics.'

Asked whether he'd keep a seagull as a pet after once declaring 'seagulls are bastards', Amit replies: 'If a seagull is a bastard, why would I keep a seagull as a pet?' He'd keep Steven Seagal as a pet instead.

Amit credits a good friend with the line 'life is not a spectator sport.' 'His name is Ajay Shah.' Yet the crew brought a football to the farm, and Ajay, who always says 'play football, don't watch football,' refuses to play.
Ajay introduces a question from 'an obscure viewer called Nomsita.' Amit: 'There's only one Nomsita in India. She's sitting behind the camera here. Hello, camera.'
Amit's farewell: 'The show will go on not because we like the show. The show will go on because we like the company.' Then, to Ajay: 'I'm not talking about you, Ajay Shah, don't be so happy.'
After the hosts agree that mortality makes everything else funny, Amit twists the show's title: 'Everything is everything and everything will die.'
On solitude, Amit says it's fine as long as it involves healthy self-reflection, 'not just basking in the melodrama of your perceived miseries as Bengalis tend to do.'
Ajay opens with an Indianised riff on the song from Shakespeare's As You Like It: 'Under the Banyan Tree, who loves to play with me, here shall she find no enemy, but summer and rough weather.'
Bob Dylan, Amit's favourite line about thoughtless lives: 'if you're not busy being born, you're busy dying.'
Andrew Breitbart's 'famous quote' that politics is downstream of culture. Amit uses it to ask whether politicians can rise above populist demand.
Douglas Adams: once he understood natural selection, there was no need to believe in God, because he'd take the awe of knowledge over the awe of ignorance any day.
Thomas Watson, president of IBM, who famously said 'I think there's a world market for three computers.' Amit cites it as a warning against judging AI by its current state.
Phineas Gage: a rod goes through his brain, damages part of it, and he becomes an entirely different person. Amit's evidence that there's no solid 'you.'
Shrayana Bhattacharya's line, via Amit: men tend to be full of unwarranted self-confidence, women full of unwarranted self-doubt.
'As Thomas Jefferson allegedly said, the price of liberty is eternal vigilance.' Amit's coda on why each generation must fight statism anew.
Ajay quotes John Lennon's 'Imagine' while arguing that borders are softening: 'imagine there's no country it's easy if you try.'
The great physicists of the early 20th century at Göttingen, who argued about the nature of matter and energy while hiking together. Ajay's example of knowledge as a social project.
Ajay on the freedom-movement generation: Gandhi as a 'black swan,' and 'the idea of Nehru sitting in a jail writing letter to his daughter, okay, it's out of the world.'

Ajay's heroes of Indian economics are the people of the sixties who challenged the establishment: Jagdish Bhagwati, T.N. Srinivasan, Anne Krueger ('Professor Krueger, for this purpose I treat you as an Indian economist'), Arun Shourie, Manmohan Singh, Montek Singh Ahluwalia and Vijay Kelkar. Amit adds Padma Desai and Isher Ahluwalia, then: 'You forgot one man. Narottam Shah.' Ajay replies that his father started CMIE, 'a grand project.'
Ajay's friend Amritha Agarwal's line on mortality: you're going into a precipitous health collapse and death with probability one. Ajay's response is to live here and find the delight of being alive.
Dan Ariely, cited by Amit as an academic who 'got into a lot of trouble' over his studies, while discussing replication problems in behavioural research.
